review.review_summary: 11 claims checked against the evidence; 5 flagged (3 unsupported, 1 contradicted, 1 overstated).
gaps: The report states OEE, availability, performance rate, and quality (first-pass yield) but provides no evidence breakdown by line or shift to identify which lines or shifts drive the overall metrics.
The report mentions MTBF (42.29 hours) in the data facts but does not analyze failures or stops by line or shift, leaving unclear which lines or shifts have the poorest reliability.
The report does not examine trends within the 3-month period (August, September, October 2026) beyond the month-over-month good count change, missing potential seasonal or drift patterns.
next_investigations: Break down OEE, availability, and performance rate by line to identify which line(s) drive the overall 70.8% OEE and whether Line B's high unplanned downtime is the primary driver.

Analyze good count and unplanned downtime by operator (groups ≥11 shifts only) to assess whether operator skill or alertness correlates with output, rather than attributing Night shift differences to alertness.
Examine failures and stops by line and machine to validate the MTBF of 42.29 hours and identify which assets are most unreliable, informing maintenance scheduling.
methodology_concerns: OEE and availability are pooled ratios summed over shifts and machines before dividing, so line-level figures aggregate multiple machines; the report does not clarify whether comparisons are fair across lines with different machine counts.

The data covers only 3 months (August–October 2026) with no same-month prior year; month-over-month changes may reflect seasonal variation rather than sustained trends, as noted in the report's own caveats.
Readings are averaged, not time-weighted; shifts or machines with different durations or frequencies may be weighted equally, potentially distorting per-shift or per-machine comparisons.

claims.text: Across 8 sensors and 3 production lines over 3 months, vibration levels and alarm rates are the primary signals to watch, with sensors S04–S06 running notably higher than the rest.
The dataset covers 17,630 readings from August through October 2026, capturing temperature, vibration, and alarm events across 3 lines and 8 sensors.
Vibration and alarms move together, and a cluster of sensors stands apart on vibration — both patterns deserve closer attention.
Sensors S04, S05, and S06 average vibration readings of 3.15, 3.21, and 3.19 mm/s respectively, while the remaining five sensors all average between 1.97 and 2.01 mm/s.
High vibration causes the alarms, so damping the line B sensors will stop them.
Temperature averages 92.4 across the three lines, with Line C the hottest by a wide margin.
264 alarms were recorded across 17,630 readings; the median reading carries no alarm, and the maximum is 1.00, confirming alarms are binary events.
Sensors S04, S05 and S06 are out of spec and the parts they monitor are defective. Addresses the clearest anomaly in the dataset before it escalates to alarms or downtime.

Review the 264 alarm events alongside their corresponding vibration readings to determine whether a vibration threshold reliably predicts alarms. Could enable earlier alarm intervention if a consistent vibration level precedes alarm events.
